content.title: Imaging for Pulmonary Embolism — V/Q, SPECT and Pulmonary Angiography (excerpt)
key_points: A three-tier V/Q scan classification is preferable: normal scan (excluding PE), high-probability scan (considered diagnostic of PE in most patients), and non-diagnostic scan.
Prospective outcome studies suggest it is safe to withhold anticoagulant therapy in patients with a normal perfusion scan; a randomized trial confirmed safety comparing V/Q scan with CTPA.
High-probability V/Q scans may confirm PE, but positive predictive value is insufficient to confirm PE in patients with low clinical probability.
Performing only a perfusion scan may be acceptable with a normal chest X-ray; a perfusion defect in that context is considered a mismatch and may warrant further testing.
High frequency of non-diagnostic scans is a limitation; incorporation of clinical probability and combined imaging strategies have been proposed to reduce nondiagnostic results.

Single-photon emission CT (SPECT) imaging (with or without low-dose CT) may decrease proportion of non-diagnostic scans (reported reductions to as low as ~5%), but many SPECT studies are limited by retrospective design or inclusion of SPECT in reference standards.
Diagnostic criteria for SPECT vary; many define PE as one or two subsegmental perfusion defects without ventilation defects, but these criteria are infrequently used in practice.

Optimal SPECT scanning technique (perfusion SPECT, V/Q SPECT, perfusion SPECT with non-enhanced CT, or V/Q SPECT with non-enhanced CT) remains undefined; few outcome studies and incomplete follow-up limit conclusions.
Pulmonary angiography was long considered the gold standard for diagnosis/exclusion of acute PE but is now rarely performed because less-invasive CTPA offers similar diagnostic accuracy.

Diagnosis of acute PE by angiography is based on direct evidence of a thrombus in two projections, either as a filling defect or as amputation of a pulmonary arterial branch; thrombi as small as ~1–2 mm in subsegmental arteries can be visualized, but interobserver variability is substantial at that level.
evidence_and_limitations: Prospective clinical outcome studies and a randomized trial support withholding anticoagulation when perfusion scan is normal.
PIOPED II analysis suggested high-probability V/Q scans could confirm PE, but other sources caution low positive predictive value in low pretest probability patients.
Many SPECT accuracy studies are retrospective or use imperfect reference standards; only one study used a validated diagnostic algorithm.
Heterogeneity in SPECT diagnostic criteria and scanning techniques complicates comparison; large-scale prospective studies are needed to validate SPECT techniques.
recommendations_implications: Use three-tier V/Q classification and incorporate clinical probability when interpreting scans.
Consider combined imaging approaches or additional testing when scans are non-diagnostic.
Recognize that CTPA is now commonly preferred over invasive pulmonary angiography for most diagnostic situations.
content.section_summary: Pulmonary angiography historically the gold standard for PE diagnosis/exclusion; now rarely performed due to less-invasive CTPA. Angiographic diagnosis requires direct visualization of thrombus in two projections; small thrombi in subsegmental arteries may be seen but with substantial interobserver variability.
